lesson.title: The Inevitable Fade: Measuring Attenuation in Decibels
lesson.summary: Every signal loses strength as it crosses a communication link, and because that loss compounds multiplicatively with distance, engineers describe it using decibels, a logarithmic unit that turns multiplication into simple addition.
lesson.body:
Every signal loses strength as it travels, whether it moves down a copper wire, through a strand of glass fiber, or across open air on a communication link. This weakening is called attenuation, and it happens because some of the signal's energy is always absorbed by the medium, as heat in a resistive copper wire, or scattered and dispersed, as light strikes microscopic impurities in a fiber, or as a radio wave spreads out in every direction. Attenuation is not a flaw in a particular cable or a sign that something is broken. It is a basic physical property of every real medium, and every network design has to account for it.

The tricky part is that attenuation is multiplicative, not additive. A signal does not lose a fixed number of watts per kilometer, it loses a fixed fraction of whatever power remains, which means the loss compounds like interest on a loan. Tracking that kind of repeated multiplication in raw power units, watts or milliwatts, is awkward, so engineers describe attenuation in decibels, where dB equals 10 times log base 10 of the ratio of output power to input power. The value of decibels is that multiplying power ratios becomes adding decibel values, so a link built from several lossy segments can have its total loss found just by summing each segment's dB loss.

Consider a real, commonly cited figure: single mode optical fiber operating at the 1550 nanometer wavelength typically attenuates light at about 0.2 dB per kilometer. Suppose an internet service provider runs a fiber link 50 kilometers from a regional hub to a neighborhood cabinet. The total attenuation is 50 km times 0.2 dB per km, or 10 dB of loss. If the laser transmitter launches the signal at 0 dBm, a power level equal to 1 milliwatt, the received power at the far end is 0 dBm minus 10 dB, or negative 10 dBm. Converting back to linear units, negative 10 dBm corresponds to 1 mW times 10 raised to the power of negative 10 divided by 10, which works out to 0.1 mW. In plain terms, a 10 dB loss means the signal arrives at only one tenth of its original power, even though the fiber itself is perfectly intact.

This is exactly why attenuation matters so much for the communication link as a whole: every link has a maximum reach beyond which the received signal becomes too weak to distinguish from the receiver's own internal noise floor, and that limit is what forces engineers to add optical amplifiers on long fiber runs, boost transmit power on wireless links, or place repeaters at regular intervals on copper cabling. Higher frequencies generally attenuate faster than lower ones in most media, one reason 5 GHz Wi-Fi covers less distance than 2.4 GHz Wi-Fi at identical transmit power, echoing the wavelength differences already described for the wireless medium.

Attenuation alone would still leave a usable, if weakened, signal at the receiver. The real trouble starts when that weakened signal has to be extracted from a background that never stays silent. As a signal's strength drops toward the level of the random disturbances riding along the same medium, it becomes harder for a receiver to tell the intended waveform apart from everything else on the line, precisely the problem that noise introduces next.
